questions.topic_text: Topic 1.6: Three-condition test for declaring dividend out of accumulated reserves - rate cap, 10% draw-down limit, 15% minimum residual reserve balance
questions.why: Rank 20 topic (Distributable Profit); Category A — 100% identical to an ICAI Study Material question; PYQ January 2026.
questions.question_html:
Figures from the financial statements of MC Limited for the year ended 31st March, 2025: Issued, Subscribed and Paid-up Share Capital – 8,00,000 Equity Shares of ₹5 each ₹40,00,000; 1,25,000, 8% Preference Shares of ₹10 each ₹12,50,000. Reserves and Surplus – Securities Premium Reserve ₹5,00,000; Capital Reserve ₹3,00,000; Capital Redemption Reserve ₹2,50,000; General Reserve ₹11,75,000. Net Profit for 2024-25 ₹2,25,000. Equity Dividend paid: 2019-20 10%, 2020-21 11%, 2021-22 12%, 2022-23 13%, 2023-24 14%. Constrained by inadequate profits in 2024-25, management proposes a dividend of 12.5% out of reserves.

You are required to ascertain the amount that can be utilized by the company out of its reserves in accordance with the Companies (Declaration of dividend out of Reserves) Rules, 2014. (4 Marks)
questions.answer_html:
Three conditions apply under the Rules: (1) Rate declared must not exceed the average of rates declared in the three years immediately preceding (2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24: average = (12%+13%+14%)/3 = 13%); the proposed 12.5% is lower, satisfying condition 1. (2) Maximum amount drawn from accumulated profits and reserves must not exceed 10% of paid-up capital and free reserves = 10% of (40,00,000+12,50,000+11,75,000) = ₹6,42,500 (as printed) – alternatively computed as 10% of ₹66,50,000 (including current year profit in free reserves) = ₹6,65,000. (3) Balance of reserves after drawal must not fall below 15% of paid-up capital = 15% of ₹52,50,000 = ₹7,87,500.

12.5% Dividend on ₹40,00,000 equity capital = ₹5,00,000. Current year profit ₹2,25,000 less 8% preference dividend on ₹12,50,000 (₹1,00,000) leaves ₹1,25,000 available from current profit; the remaining ₹3,75,000 must come from accumulated reserves. Since all three conditions are satisfied and the required ₹5,00,000 (or, on the alternative computation, ₹3,75,000 needed against a maximum usable ₹6,12,500 after maintaining the 15% minimum reserve balance) is within the permitted limits, the company can utilize ₹5,00,000 in total (₹1,25,000 from current year profit and ₹3,75,000 from accumulated reserves) as per the Companies (Declaration of Dividend out of Reserves) Rules, 2014.
questions.mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees were unfamiliar with the three conditions for declaring dividends from accumulated profits. They failed to compute the dividend amount correctly. While some examinees were able to apply the provisions relating to declaration of dividend under the Companies (Declaration of Dividend out of Reserves) Rules, 2014, several committed errors in determining the distributable amount and related adjustments. Although many could correctly calculate the average rate of dividend for the preceding three years and the dividend on preference shares, they failed to correctly apply the limits of 10% and 15%.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.6: Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014 - three-condition test for drawing dividend from accumulated reserves, excluding Revaluation Reserve from free reserves
questions.why: Rank 20 topic (Distributable Profit); Category A — 100% identical to an ICAI Study Material question; PYQ May 2025.
questions.question_html:
Due to inadequacy of profits during the year ended 31st March, 2025, DAY Ltd proposes to declare 9% dividend out of General reserves. From the following particulars, ascertain the amount that can be utilized from the General reserves according to the Companies (Declaration of dividend) rules, 2014.

9,50,000 Equity Shares of ₹10 each fully paid up ₹95,00,000; General reserves as on 1st April, 2024 ₹18,50,000; Revaluation Reserve as on 1st April, 2024 ₹4,25,000; Net profit for the year ended 31st March, 2025 ₹3,75,000; Average rate of dividend during the last 3 years has been 12.5%. (4 Marks)
questions.answer_html:
Amount that can be drawn from reserves for 9% dividend: 9% dividend on ₹95,00,000 = ₹8,55,000; less current year profit available (₹3,75,000) = amount which can be utilised from reserves ₹4,80,000.

Conditions per Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014:

Condition I: Since 9% is lower than the average rate of dividend (12.5%), 9% dividend can be declared — satisfied.

Condition II: Maximum amount that can be drawn from accumulated profits and reserves must not exceed 10% of paid-up capital plus free reserves, i.e. ₹11,35,000 [10% of (95,00,000+18,50,000)] — satisfied.

Condition III: The balance of reserves after drawal, ₹13,70,000 (₹18,50,000−₹4,80,000), must not fall below 15% of paid up capital, i.e. ₹14,25,000 (15% of ₹95,00,000) — NOT satisfied.

Conclusion: Since Condition III is not satisfied, DAY Ltd cannot declare dividend @ 9%. For all three conditions to be satisfied, DAY Ltd. can maximum utilize ₹4,25,000 (bringing General Reserve down to exactly ₹14,25,000, the 15% floor) and pay dividend only to that extent. (Revaluation Reserve is not a Free Reserve and is excluded from this computation throughout.)
questions.mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees were unfamiliar with the three conditions for declaring dividends from accumulated profits. They failed to compute the dividend amount correctly. Some incorrectly considered Revaluation Reserves as Free Reserves, which led to wrong calculations of available profits and post-withdrawal reserve balances. As a result, they could not determine the permissible withdrawal from General Reserves under the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.1: Meaning of Company - the five cumulative conditions defining a Small and Medium-Sized Company (SMC) under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021
questions.why: Rank 45 topic (Meaning of Company); PYQ November 2023.
questions.question_html: List down the applicable criteria under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, to classify a company as Small and Medium Sized Company (SMC).
questions.answer_html:
Criteria for classification of Companies under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021 to classify a company as Small and Medium-Sized Company (SMC):

“Small and Medium Sized Company” (SMC) means, a company –

(i) whose equity or debt securities are not listed or are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange, whether in India or outside India;

(ii) which is not a bank, financial institution or an insurance company;

(iii) whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed rupees two-fifty crores in the immediately preceding accounting year;

(iv) which does not have borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees fifty crores at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and

(v) which is not a holding or subsidiary company of a company which is not a small and medium-sized company.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A few examinees omitted one or more of the five cumulative SMC conditions, most often the borrowings ceiling and the holding/subsidiary-company condition, recalling only the more commonly cited listing-status and turnover criteria.
